newsitem.title: USA: Tips to make discount shopping easier.
newsitem.headline: Tips to make discount shopping easier.

text.p: What is fit punishment for the last-minute shopper? Having to pay full retail prices.
So says the co-author of a new how-to book, "Buying retail is stupid - USA" (Contemporary Books, Chicago, $14.95).

"The only time you have to buy retail is due to poor planning, when it's the last minute. You spend the most money; they get you that way," said Trisha King, a Southern California-based newspaper columnist and co-author with Deborah Newmark of the new guide.
Bargain shopping takes some time to get organised, but once you do, you should be able to do a year's worth of shopping at one time. And time is indeed money.
For example, King said, at the beginning of the year buy all of your cards at the same time. Buy all of your wrapping paper and ribbons as well.
"It takes about an hour each time you have to go to a store to buy wrapping and a card. Let's say you give about 25 to 30 gifts a year. That's one whole day you've saved," she said.

She also advocated shopping year around for everything. If you see a purple sweater for your purple sweater-loving aunt in December but her birthday isn't until April, by all means buy it and put it away.
"Regardless of where you shop, you have to be a smart shopper. A sign (such as "outlet" or "discount") means nothing," she said.
King urged caution when going to manufacturer's outlet malls, where the unwary consumer might belive that everything is either an irregular (not true) or at a discounted price (not true either).
"Many shoppers go into (outlet malls) in a shark feeding frenzy," buying everything in sight. "Not everything there is a bargain."

Another myth King would like to dispell is that "you have to go to the ends of the earth. You can find discounts and bargains in your neighbourhood," she said. Check phone books, local newspapers and with other value-conscious shoppers.

Outlet malls are still a growing trend in this country but King said it was unlikely that all the items offered were overstocks, as many outlets claim. Using the example of a men's and boyswear manufacturer, "they can't have enough overrun to fill 200 outlet stores," she said.
Often, the items offered are made specifically for the outlet shops and can be different in quality from the department store items of the same brand name.
A true factory outlet is on the premises of a factory, she said. "When you're seeing real samples, it's an outlet store."

A bargain hunter's best friend are often newspaper advertisements for major retailers and department stores. These give shoppers an easy way to compare prices for brand name items, or help shoppers organise shopping trips.
King also advised taking pencil, paper and calculator to figure out unit prices to assure you're getting the cheapest item by volume or weight. Also, watch the scanner for errors at the checkout.
Planning and research may lead you to such bargain havens as swap meets, flea markets and resale shops, where little or never worn items are offered at a fraction of original prices.
Even if something has a fancy label, carefully examine the garment for rips and stains, King advised.
Mail order is another good way to keep shopping hours to a minimum. What you save in gas, tolls and hours on the freeway may balance out the few extra pennies an item may, or may not, cost.
